newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Transport ministers back EU hard line with Swiss.
newsitem.headline: Transport ministers back EU hard line with Swiss.

text.p: European Union transport ministers on Friday threw their support behind the 15-nation bloc's robust negotiating position on access for heavy vehicles passing through Switzerland.

"No one is in favour of a levy of 600 Swiss francs ($423) (per truck). I think it is a prohibitive levy," Dutch Transport Minister Annemarie Jorritsma told a news conference in Amsterdam after the first day of a two-day EU informal transport council hosted by the Netherlands.
Switzerland last week proposed the 600 franc charge as the price to be paid for lifting its current ban on vehicles exceeding 28 tonnes.
The EU wants Switzerland to allow in 40-tonne trucks which now must go through France and Austria to cross the Alps.
European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said he respected the arithmetic of the Swiss, but reiterated his statement of last week that the proposed charge was prohibitive.
"Six hundred Swiss francs for crossing Switzerland is not even a figure to start talking about," he said.
EU ministers nevertheless agreed that a resolution of the dispute was a matter of urgency.
"We are looking for a satisfactory agreement in the early months of this year," Kinnock said.

He said Friday's ministerial meeting had produce a range of ideas that should comfort Swiss sensitivities, but he would not give details, saying it would be inappropriate to reveal the EU's hand at this stage.
"We're not very much inclined to go into great detail as ... that would spoil the nice surprises we have for them," he said.
Transport ministers also agreed that EU members should proceed with haste in developing a common system of electronic road tolls.
"A certain degree of urgency is required...The point simply is to avoid the incompatibility we saw (in the development) of televisions ..(or) mobile phones," Jorritsma said.

Kinnock added that while countries would not be forced to adopt road tolls, those that decided to do so would be urged to adopt the common system. "The fact that some countries are already operating (a given toll system) will not mean that they be excluded from an interoperable system," he said.
On Saturday, the informal committee will conclude with talks on air traffic management, the third issue on the Dutch agenda.
The two-day informal council comes under the aegis of the Netherlands' six month presidency of the European Union.
